newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU seeks ban on suspect BSE sheep tissue.
newsitem.headline: EU seeks ban on suspect BSE sheep tissue.

text.p: The European Union's executive commission finalised a proposal on Tuesday to ban tissue from sheep and goats, as well as cattle, most likely to be infected with scrapie or mad cow disease.

The proposal, which was overwhelmingly rejected last week by the EU's Standing Veterinary Committee, was adopted without discussion at the Commission's weekly meeting in Strasbourg and will be sent to an EU farm ministers' meeting on December 16-17.
"Protection of human health and the restoration of consumer confidence in beef and sheepmeat must be a top priority," EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler said in a statement.
"It is regrettable therefore that the Standing Veterinary Committee voted against the proposed ban," Fischler added.

Twelve national veterinary officials voted against the ban, arguing that their countries were virtually free from mad cow disease, or bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), and that the measures were therefore economically unjustified.
Only Britain and France voted in favour. Ireland abstained.
The proposal is for the removal of the brains, eyes, spinal cord and spleen from sheep, goats and cattle over 12 months old and their exclusion from human and animal food.
BSE is believed to have arisen from sheep scrapie, a similar brain-wasting disease, which can be passed from one animal to another and from ewe to lamb but not to humans.

But recent British and French research has shown that sheep could catch BSE which can be transmitted to humans. Sheep have also been fed on meat and bone meal, which is believed to be a prime cause of BSE.
